title: Concerning Mixed Principalities
coreMove: Stabilize an annexation by limiting new injuries, staying near disorders, and blocking stronger outsiders before resentment matures.
sourcePressure: The source treats mixed principalities as transition systems full of injured locals, disappointed helpers, language and law differences, absent rulers, garrisons, colonies, minor powers, foreign entrants, and deferred wars. Louis XII loses Milan because he strengthens larger powers, admits Spain, fails to reside, fails to plant colonies, and mishandles regional balance.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version says people hate change. The writer must preserve the specific machinery: new subjects suffer burdens, old allies are disappointed, residence sees trouble early, colonies injure fewer than garrisons, minor powers must be protected without strengthening them, and a foreign power must not be invited in.

hook: a generic leader promising change will be hard
a conqueror celebrating victory as if the problem is over
counterintuition: most people assume conquest ends the problem, but actually transition begins it
change management is really about empathy
war should always be avoided because time heals tensions
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds and list people who dislike change

exampleSpecs.domain: a postwar civilian authority annexing a port district with a different language and tax code
exampleSpecs.audience: an administrator deciding between governing from the capital or moving into the port
exampleSpecs.stakes: dockworkers who opened the gates expect relief, warehouse owners fear confiscation, and distant officials will hear of riots only after they are organized
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: She folds the capital-office lease, pins a desk tag inside the port customs house, and watches the first tax protest form while it is still three men at a counter.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A customs-house desk tag lies beside a bilingual tax ledger.

exampleSpecs.domain: a rail authority absorbing an independent mountain line after its board invited help
exampleSpecs.audience: a transport commissioner tempted to fill every station with armed fare inspectors
exampleSpecs.stakes: the old board expected investment, riders expected lower fares, and a roaming enforcement force would make every village feel conquered
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The commissioner moves six brass station keys from the garrison request onto two permanent depot posts, showing the choice to plant small local presence instead of sending inspectors up and down the line.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Six brass station keys sit on top of an enforcement requisition.

exampleSpecs.domain: a river-delta protectorate managing minor chiefs after a neighboring empire offers them troops
exampleSpecs.audience: a resident envoy balancing local allies against a stronger outside power
exampleSpecs.stakes: weak chiefs can help hold the delta only if they are protected without being enlarged enough to challenge the protectorate
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The envoy asks which chief should receive the seized patrol boats, then turns the boats' nameplates face down and instead assigns escort schedules that protect each chief without adding territory.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Patrol-boat nameplates are stacked beside a river-delta chart.

exampleSpecs.domain: a provincial health ministry taking over a border hospital network that kept its own hiring rules
exampleSpecs.audience: a minister deciding whether to replace local rules immediately after acquisition
exampleSpecs.stakes: patients want better supplies, nurses fear lost seniority, and altering pay tables before trust forms could turn a welcomed takeover into a hostile one
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before issuing the standard pay grid, the minister sets the old seniority cards beside the provincial salary sheet and stamps only the medicine-supply order for the first week.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Old seniority cards fan out beside a provincial salary sheet.

exampleSpecs.domain: a desert oasis district added to an old kingdom after local merchants funded the campaign
exampleSpecs.audience: a tax governor trying to satisfy merchants who helped him enter the district
exampleSpecs.stakes: the merchants want monopoly privileges, farmers fear new levies, and the governor cannot crush allies he still depends on
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: When the merchants slide a monopoly charter across the date table, the governor places it beside the farmers' water-tax tablets and marks both as injuries that would create enemies if granted whole.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A folded monopoly charter rests beside clay water-tax tablets.

exampleSpecs.domain: a league of city-states deciding whether to invite a distant kingdom to counter a rival after annexing a valley
exampleSpecs.audience: councillors tempted to divide the valley question with a powerful outsider to avoid immediate war
exampleSpecs.stakes: sharing control may postpone fighting but gives every malcontent a stronger patron and may make the outsider master of the whole region
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The clerk draws arrows from the valley rebels to the distant king's seal, then writes deferred war on the margin where the council had written avoided war.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A distant king's seal is pressed into the corner of a valley map.

skillTargets: diagnose the two early enemy groups in a mixed principality: injured locals and disappointed helpers
choose between residence, colonies, garrisons, preserving laws and taxes, and regional balance in scenario terms
analyze how helping a greater power or admitting a foreign power weakens the new holder
evaluate whether avoiding a present war merely defers it to another power's advantage

tryThisNowSpec: Pick a recent annexation, takeover, or occupation from public affairs. Write the first four pressures: who was injured, which helpers expected reward, which local rules are dangerous to touch, and what outside power could be invited in.
